part_flow.title: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models
part_flow.contribution: In a model neural circuit, a pattern of firing rates across many nerve cells can represent a remembered angle. Random spike timing can change that angle while activity persists. The central source, [Burak and Fiete (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109), derives how quickly accuracy can be lost and how well the value can be read. Chapters 1 and 2 establish the background. Chapters 3 and 5 develop the central diffusion and information results. Chapters 4 and 6 explain long-delay behavior and readout. Expanded examples and marked checks of printed formulas are guide-derived.
part_flow.connection_reason: Starts with physical spike/state meanings before stability and precision limits. This supplies the quantities that the observations later measure or use.

part_flow.title: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code
part_flow.contribution: These studies connect neural activity to eye control in monkeys and location in rodents and bats. [Ben-Shushan et al. (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y) supply the central shared-drive inference and a possible integrator explanation in Chapters 7 to 9. [Mainali et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017) supply the spatial model, field-size predictions, and supporting shape tests in Chapters 10 to 12. Chapter 13 is a guide-derived comparison of those results with Burak and Fiete (2012). The eye chapters begin with recordings and then test a possible neural source. The place chapters begin with a spatial input model and then test its field statistics.
part_flow.connection_reason: Moves from theory to recorded behavior and static spatial patterns. Its opening explicitly tells readers that eye source inference and place statistics test different parts; synthesis follows both.

part_flow.title: Neural memory in electronic hardware
part_flow.contribution: Electronic circuits can store connection settings, changing neuron states, and values represented by a network. Von Neumann (1958) motivates this comparison. Chapters 14 and 15 connect physical storage with Seung (1996) and Burak and Fiete (2012). Chapter 16 examines the separate contributions of selected hardware studies through October 30, 2026. Chapter 17 develops guide-derived experiments using the three original papers. Each contribution is attributed in the Part introduction.
part_flow.connection_reason: Changes physical implementation after defining neural state and evidence. Its opening defines the weight/state/value distinctions again for electronics before architecture comparisons.

part_flow.title: Simulations connect model assumptions to measurable outcomes
part_flow.contribution: [Burak and Fiete (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109) test memory diffusion in spiking networks. [Ben-Shushan et al. (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y) connect a simulated neural command to eye motion. [Mainali et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017) generate spatial maps and compare their fields with recordings. This Part explains the methods, measurements, and software behind those studies, then gives a guide-derived route for checking a reproduction.
part_flow.connection_reason: Returns to original papers at numerical-method level after all physical questions. Explicit paper-specific new tasks prevent this from being a second beginner mechanism pass.

special_route_checks.answer: The short route supplies the concepts actually used by Chapter10. Gaussian-map definitions and new derivative conditions are taught there, so the route need not require eye mechanics, full attractor projection or readout proofs. Later topology and limiting size laws receive their own teaching in11-12.

Orientation first states each study question, operation and result, then explicitly distinguishes model assumptions, derived prediction, simulation and animal data. The native evidence table reads down each paper separately and ends with what remains unknown. Synthesis uses that separation to propose, rather than assume, a cross-paper link.

Chapter1 secFOUNDATIONS-SIMULATION follows state/rate/count teaching with the actual s-update and how theory is compared with generated trajectories. This is needed before projection and diffusion theory. Chapter18 explicitly adds source parameters, maximum-rate-versus-theoretical-coordinate measurement, rate/activation units and open implementation choices. Chapters19-21 add saved samples, code/data routes, detector conventions and resolution checks. The late Part is methods depth, with a stated new task, not deferred essential mechanism.

order_alternative_considered.alternative: Place PartIV before hardware, or insert each simulation-method chapter directly after its source-paper chapter.
order_alternative_considered.benefit: Could shorten the jump from a particular paper to its exact numerical settings and code route.
order_alternative_considered.cost_and_decision: Current earlier chapters already teach the required simulation mechanism and explain what tests establish; hardware protocol17 defines its own decoder and sampling checks. No prerequisite currently depends on later file names or package defaults. Interleaving detailed reproduction settings would interrupt the theory-to-empirical-to-synthesis progression. Keep current order; no required move is justified.
